newsitem.title: USA: British Airways selling stake in USAir.
newsitem.headline: British Airways selling stake in USAir.

text.p: British Airways put its 24.6 percent stake in USAir Group Inc. up for sale Wednesday in the beginning of the end of its unhappy marriage with the U.S. airline, prompting forecasts of a bumpy ride ahead for USAir.

The move had been expected since the two airlines fell out this year over British Airway's plans to link up with the much bigger American Airlines. USAir is suing British Airways in a U.S. federal court over those plans, alleging breach of agreement.

The Arlington, Va.-based domestic airline must now confront the tough job of securing new international partners or face possible takeover pressure, analysts said following British Airways' announcement.

British Airways said in a statement that, if USAir did not exercise its option to buy back the stake within 60 days, then the powerful British airline will make a public offering. British Airways bought the stake -- in the form of convertible bonds -- for $400 million in 1993.
The three British Airways directors on USAir's board will resign once the sale is completed.

"British Airways has taken this action with regret. But it has become inevitable. It would clearly be unwise to pursue an alliance with an unwilling partner," British Airways Chief Executive Bob Ayling said in a statement.
Ayling said the decision to sell was not related to the lawsuit, which he said British Airways believed was groundless.

In its statement on the pending divorce, USAir said, "This is an important first step that USAir has been seeking in order for it to become an effective, independent competitor to London's Heathrow airport."
But, because nearly a fourth of USAir stock may be up for grabs, some analysts think USAir will become a prime takeover target.
"It certainly moves USAir to the centre of the radar screen," said Tom Schreier, an airline analyst with the CS First Boston Corp. investment bank.

USAir will, however, have a say in its own fate since British Airways cannot sell its 24.6 percent USAir holding to one buyer. Under its agreement with USAir, British Airways can not sell its stake to any entity that would gain more than 5 percent of USAir stock -- unless USAir approved the deal, Schreier said.
Although USAir said it was committed to remaining independent, analysts said it may be more receptive to a partnership once it faces the lonely battle of trying to expand internationally.
Unless USAir gains access to Heathrow, the airline will have a tough time competing against other domestic carriers that have forged strong trans-Atlantic ties, analysts said.

"You don't do things by yourself these days. You can't do the things (USAir Chairman Stephen) Wolf wants to do -- as far as resurrecting USAir -- without some kind of alliances," said Dick Henderson, an airline analyst with Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette.
"Wolf's experience with long-haul carriers means he knows all the international players and the contacts, which he may reach out to," Henderson said.
But many of the viable international airlines are already married to U.S. carriers.
"There's not many international players left to create another alliance" that would replace its relationship with British Airways, said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read & Co.
As competition heats up in European markets, carriers there may look for more than one U.S. partner over the long term, Henderson said.
"There's pressure on European carriers to compete against British Airways. USAir has a strong East Coast route structure that would make them an attractive partner," Henderson said.

USAir has applied to operate its own trans-Atlantic routes but it will not be able to secure access to Heathrow without a U.S.-British agreement on a new "open skies" aviation pact. That agreement, in turn, has been linked to approval of the British Airways-American Airlines deal.

"Once USAir is out of this tie-up with BA, they are clear to start flying the Atlantic, if they can get the slots at Heathrow under an open skies agreement," said one industry executive with a rival U.S. airline, who declined to be identified.

"What they will be saying now is 'We can't let the BA/American deal fall through because if it does, there won't be open skies and our trans-Atlantic plans fall with it.' So I think we will see a subtle change in USAir's position on the BA/American deal."
Wednesday's move raised hopes that by cutting USAir loose, British Airways and American had improved their chances of winning U.S. regulatory approval of their deal.
Analysts, however, warned that British Airways risked winding up alone in the all-important trans-Atlantic market if that deal fell through.
